facts.a: Pizza as we know it grew up in Naples in the 1700s and 1800s as cheap street food for the working poor - flatbreads sold from stalls and eaten folded, standing up. Tomatoes, once feared as poisonous, joined in the eighteenth century, and the modern topped pizza crystallized there. Flatbreads are ancient and universal; the tomato-topped pizza is specifically Neapolitan.
alt: Naples, roughly the eighteenth century onward. It was food for the lazzaroni - the city's poor - sold by street vendors, often on credit. The tomato's arrival from the Americas turned an old flatbread habit into the dish the whole world now argues about.

Flatbread is as old as ovens, but pizza - the tomato-sauced, topped, folded Neapolitan kind - is a product of Naples' crowded streets in the 1700s-1800s. It stayed a local secret remarkably long; northern Italians barely touched it until the twentieth century.

Let me correct a common one first: pizza was not invented in ancient Rome or Egypt. Those cultures baked flatbreads, and flatbread is not pizza. The dish we mean - a tomato-topped, folded Neapolitan bread sold on the street - was born in Naples in the 1700s and 1800s, food for the city's poor, the lazzaroni. Ancient ovens made bread; Naples made pizza.

facts.a: The legend: in 1889, pizzaiolo Raffaele Esposito made three pizzas for Queen Margherita of Savoy, who favored the tomato-mozzarella-basil one in the colors of the flag, and it took her name. The reality check: historians have found tomato-mozzarella-basil pizzas described decades earlier, and the famous thank-you letter from the royal household has serious authenticity problems. Great story, shaky paperwork - I tell it anyway, with a wink.
alt: As the story goes, Esposito of Pizzeria Brandi presented the queen a tricolore pizza in 1889 and christened it Margherita. Scholars point out the combination existed well before, and the celebrated royal letter looks doctored. The truth is probably that a good marketer met a good pizza - the second-oldest tradition in Naples.

It's the founding myth of modern pizza: queen visits Naples, prefers the flag-colored pie, name sticks. Delightful, and mostly unverifiable - the topping combo predates 1889 and the documentary evidence wobbles. File under 'print the legend'.

Let me separate documented from myth. Documented: tomato-mozzarella-basil pizzas existed in Naples decades before 1889. Not reliably documented: that Raffaele Esposito of Pizzeria Brandi invented that pizza for Queen Margherita in 1889 - the royal thank-you letter at the heart of the story has serious authenticity problems. So 'the Margherita was invented for the queen in 1889' is a legend, not a fact. The name may date from around then; the pizza does not.

alt: Marinara, by decades. The garlic-oregano-tomato pie was already the Naples staple in the early nineteenth century; cheese came later as the upgrade. So the 'basic' pizza on every menu is actually the ancestral one.

No seafood - that is the first thing to clear up. A pizza marinara is tomato, garlic, oregano, and olive oil, nothing from the sea. The name comes from the marinai, the sailors, whose wives could keep those shelf-stable ingredients at home. And it is the older pizza: the standard Neapolitan pie in the early 1800s, decades before the Margherita and its mozzarella.

Two misconceptions in one question, so let me refuse both. Marinara is not named after seafood and has none on it - it is tomato, garlic, oregano, and oil, named for the sailors' families who ate it. And marinara is not a stripped-down Margherita; it is the ancestor. It was the Neapolitan standard by the early nineteenth century; mozzarella, and with it the Margherita, came along later.

facts.a: Tomatoes reached Europe from the Americas in the 1500s but spent over a century as an ornamental curiosity - as a nightshade relative they were widely suspected of being poisonous, and acidic tomato juice leaching lead from pewter plates didn't help the reputation. Southern Italy's poor, eating from wooden plates, adopted them first; by the 1700s the tomato had found the Neapolitan flatbread, and history pivoted.
alt: Sixteenth century, via the Spanish from the New World - then a hundred-plus years of being grown for looks while people feared the nightshade family. Naples' poor had nothing to lose and no pewter to poison them, so the south embraced it first. The pizza was waiting.

Not native, and not ancient - two corrections at once. The tomato is American; it crossed to Europe with the Spanish in the 1500s, so no Roman ever put one on a flatbread. Then it sat for more than a century as a garden curiosity, feared as a poisonous nightshade, its acid pulling lead from pewter plates to seal the reputation. Naples' poor, eating off wood, embraced it, and by the 1700s it was on their flatbread.

The flatbread came first; the tomato joined it. People assume pizza and tomato were born together, but the bread habit in Naples is older than the tomato's arrival in Europe in the sixteenth century, and much older than its acceptance as food. For over a century Europeans grew tomatoes for looks and feared them as poisonous nightshade. Southern Italy's poor broke the taboo, and in the 1700s the tomato met the Neapolitan flatbread.

Not New York, and not Brandi - Naples, and Antica Pizzeria Port'Alba. It is credited as the first true pizzeria: a street stand from 1738, a place with seats from 1830. By the middle of the 1800s Naples had a whole trade of pizzaioli while the rest of Italy had none. Brandi, Da Michele, and Sorbillo are historic houses and still bake, but the 'first' title belongs to Port'Alba.

Two dates matter, and both belong to Port'Alba in Naples: 1738, when it sold pizza from a stand, and 1830, when it sat customers down and became a pizzeria in the modern sense. If someone tells you the first pizzeria was an American one, they are off by more than a century and a half - America's first, Lombardi's, only opened in 1905. Several of Naples' old houses are still in business, which is its own kind of proof.

The order surprises people, so let me set it straight: pizza did not conquer Italy first and then the world. It went Naples to New York, in the luggage of emigrants around 1900, while Milan and Turin were still ignoring it. Lombardi's in Manhattan, licensed in 1905, is the canonical first American pizzeria. Then the war: in 1945 American soldiers came home from the Italian campaign hungry for what they had eaten near Naples, and the craze went global.

Emigration did it, not marketing. Around 1900 Neapolitans crossed the Atlantic in steerage and opened pizzerias in New York - Lombardi's, 1905, holds the first-in-America title. Northern Italy came later, not earlier: pizza was American before it was Milanese. The second wave came in 1945, when GIs returning from Italy asked for pizza at home, and the dish never looked back.

Where the word came from before that is argued: Greek 'pitta' has supporters, so does a Langobardic 'bizzo' meaning bite. Older than the dish by centuries - that is the part people get backwards. The word is not eighteenth-century Neapolitan; it is on paper in 997 AD, in Gaeta, in Latin, seven centuries before the tomato-topped pizza existed. Whatever those medieval pizze were, they were not what we eat now. As for the deeper root, Greek pitta and Germanic bizzo are the leading candidates and the matter is unsettled - I give you the candidates, not a verdict.

facts.a: Tarte flambée comes from the farmhouses of Alsace, on the French-German border. Baking day started with a roaring oven far too hot for bread, so farmers rolled scraps of dough thin, spread them with cream, onion, and lardons, and used them to gauge the falling heat - 'flambée' because the flames still licked the oven. The oven test became the delicacy.
alt: Alsace - and it began as instrumentation, not cuisine: a thin test flatbread thrown into a freshly fired bread oven to judge when the temperature had fallen enough for loaves. If it baked in two minutes, too hot for bread, perfect for tarte. Breakfast for the baker, then a restaurant staple from the 1960s on.

Alsace, and it is not an Italian import - tarte flambée, Flammkuchen in German, grew out of the farmhouse bread oven, not out of any pizzeria. On baking day the freshly fired oven was too hot for loaves, so the farmer stretched a scrap of dough thin, topped it with cream, onion, and lardons, and slid it in to read the heat: if it was done in two minutes, wait a little longer for the bread. The flames still licking the walls gave it the name.

The name misleads people: nothing is set alight. 'Flambée' means the oven was still flaming when the tart went in, because it was baked first, in the blaze that precedes bread. Alsatian farmers used that thin cream-and-onion flatbread as a thermometer for the oven, ate it for breakfast, and did not think of it as cuisine at all. Restaurants adopted it from the 1960s, and now the thermometer is on every menu in Strasbourg.

facts.a: Rome came to pizza late - largely twentieth century - and shaped it to its own taste: thinner, crisper, baked in the electric deck ovens of urban pizzerias rather than wood domes. Without Naples' rulebook, Rome allowed oil in the dough and the rolling pin, and invented its own canon: the tonda scrocchiarella in the evening, al taglio by the slice all day. Same dish, opposite temperament.
alt: Roman pizza is essentially a modern city's edit of a Neapolitan classic: adopted in the 1900s, adapted to electric ovens and Roman preference for crunch. No STG rules meant freedom - oil, rolling pins, cracker-thin bases - and later the al taglio counter culture that Bonci elevated to an art form.

Not ancient - that needs saying because the word 'Roman' fools people. Rome's pizza tradition is a twentieth-century one. The city took the Neapolitan dish and edited it for its own taste and its own ovens: electric decks in urban pizzerias instead of wood domes, a rolling pin and oil in the dough that Naples' rulebook forbids, and a cracker-crisp result. Out of that came the tonda for the evening and al taglio by the slice, which Gabriele Bonci later turned into a craft.

Late to the party, not first at it - that is Rome. Naples had pizzerias in the 1700s; Rome's pizza culture is mostly a product of the 1900s, built in electric-oven neighborhood pizzerias rather than around wood fires. Free of any STG rules, Roman bakers added oil, reached for the rolling pin, and chased crunch - the scrocchiarella. Al taglio, the slab sold by the slice, grew up alongside it and became an art in Bonci's hands.

Pinsa is not ancient Roman, and it is not the ancestor of pizza. The legend of legionaries, Virgil, and ancestral grain cakes was written afterwards to sell it. Pizza itself is older than pinsa by two centuries. Enjoy the pinsa - it is a good, light base - but read the menu's history paragraph as advertising.

If a menu tells you pinsa was eaten by Roman legions or mentioned by Virgil, that is marketing copy, not history, and I say so every time. The dish dates from about 2001 and belongs to Corrado Di Marco's company, which owns the flour mix - wheat, rice, and soy. The ancient backstory was constructed for the launch. It worked: within twenty years pinserias were everywhere quoting Latin. Good product, invented tradition.

Not from Hawaii - that is the part everyone gets wrong. The Hawaiian pizza was invented in Canada, in 1962, by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek-born restaurateur at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario. Ontario, Canada, 1962, Sam Panopoulos. If someone tells you it is a Hawaiian island tradition, they are wrong - it never came anywhere near Honolulu. Neither rule you have heard is true. It is not rude to eat pizza with your hands in Italy - folding a slice, or folding the whole pizza into quarters 'a libretto' for the street, is pure Naples. Picture the table in Naples: each person gets a whole, uncut pizza and a knife and fork. You cut from the edge, and when the slice is manageable you may well pick it up and fold it - hands are entirely acceptable. On the street it is the libretto: fold the whole pizza in four and eat it walking. What you will not see is a shared, pre-cut pizza in the middle of the table; that sharing culture is an export invention.

facts.a: A pizzaiolo (Neapolitan: pizzaiuolo) is the pizza maker - and in Naples it's a craft identity with rank and lineage, traditionally learned from apprenticeship as a boy. UNESCO's 2017 listing honors exactly this: the gestures, the dough-slapping, the oven judgment, the neighborhood theater of it. The dough recipe takes an afternoon to learn and the hands take years.
alt: The pizza maker - but in Naples the word carries the weight 'sommelier' does elsewhere: a recognized craft with masters, apprentices, and dynasties. What UNESCO protected in 2017 wasn't the recipe, it was this human transmission chain.

Pizzaiolo - pizzaiuolo in Neapolitan - means the pizza maker, and in Naples that is a craft with rank, lineage, and masters, learned by apprenticeship from boyhood. One correction: UNESCO did not list the pizza or its recipe. What it inscribed in 2017 was the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo - the hand gestures, the dough-slapping, the oven judgment, the neighborhood theater. The recipe takes an afternoon; the hands take years, and that is what was protected.

Think of it as a title, not a job description. The pizzaiolo is the pizza maker, but Naples uses the word the way others use 'sommelier' - a recognized craft with masters, apprentices, and family dynasties. When UNESCO listed the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo in 2017, it was honoring that human chain of transmission, not a recipe and not a dish. Anyone can copy a dough formula in an afternoon; nobody copies the hands without years.

facts.a: In order: marinara, then Margherita, then export. The marinara - tomato, garlic, oregano, oil - was the Neapolitan standard by the early 1800s. The Margherita, with mozzarella and basil, takes its name from the 1889 legend of Queen Margherita, though the topping combination is documented decades earlier. Export came last: Neapolitan emigrants carried pizza to New York around 1900, and Lombardi's opened there in 1905. Roughly a century from the first marinara to the first American pizzeria.
alt: Marinara first, Margherita second, America third - and anyone who tells you the Margherita is the original has it backwards. Early nineteenth century: marinara is the everyday Naples pizza. Late nineteenth century, 1889 by the legend: the Margherita gets its royal name, though the tomato-mozzarella-basil pizza was already around. Turn of the twentieth century: emigrants take pizza across the Atlantic, Lombardi's licensed in 1905. Naples had the whole canon before New York had a single pizzeria.

Think of it as three steps a few decades apart. Step one, the early 1800s: marinara, the garlic-and-oregano pie, feeding Naples' poor. Step two, the late 1800s: the Margherita, named in the 1889 queen story, mozzarella joining the tomato. Step three, around 1900: emigration, with Lombardi's in Manhattan by 1905 as America's first pizzeria. So no, pizza did not reach America before the Margherita existed; the Margherita was named about a decade and a half before the first American pizzeria.

The order people guess is usually wrong, so here is the real one. The marinara came first - Naples' standard pizza in the early 1800s, decades before mozzarella was routine. The Margherita is younger: the queen legend dates it to 1889, and while the topping predates that year, the name and fame do not. Pizza's export is the last chapter, around 1900, with Lombardi's opening in New York in 1905. From marinara to Manhattan is about a hundred years, all of it spent in Naples.
